_style: Write standard, polite, warm Burmese in Unicode (never Zawgyi), in a gentle colloquial-written register like good Myanmar apps: not stiff literary (သည်/၏ only where needed for clarity), not slangy. Address the user as “သင်” (possessive “သင့်”) and use polite endings (…ပါ, …နော်) sparingly; the couple is “သင်တို့နှစ်ယောက်”, and when the user speaks to the partner in their own words (messages, letters, reactions) use “ကိုယ်” or omit the pronoun. The partner is always “ချစ်သူ” / “သင့်ချစ်သူ” — never ယောက်ျားလေး/မိန်းကလေး, ကောင်လေး/ကောင်မလေး, ခင်ပွန်း/ဇနီး, ကိုကို/မမ, သူ/သူမ by gender: Burmese is naturally gender-neutral, so repeat “ချစ်သူ” or omit the subject instead of using သူမ. A partner's name placeholder (%@) is never altered or inflected: attach particles after it with a space where natural (“%@ က”, “%@ ကို”, “%@ ရဲ့”) and rephrase if a sentence would need the name changed. Quotes are curly “ ” (inner ‘ ’); end sentences with ။ and use ၊ for clause commas, but keep !, ?, …, “ · ” and \n exactly as in the source and put no space before ။ ၊ ! ?. Use spaces only between phrases (not between every syllable) so lines break well. Keep every format specifier (%@, %lld, %1$@ …) and let the system format numbers and dates; avoid hard-coding numbers, and write a literal number that must appear in Latin digits 0–9: the app formats numbers in Burmese with Latin digits, because the rounded bold system font draws the Burmese digits ၂ and ၅ broken, and keep brand/product names in Latin script (Coupley, Premium, AI, CoupleSync, iCloud). Burmese has no capital letters: buttons are short verb phrases ending in “ရန်” or a bare verb (“သိမ်းရန်”, “ပို့ရန်”, “ထပ်ကြိုးစားရန်”), tabs and chips are 1–2 words, titles are short noun phrases without ending ။. Plural category is only “other” (Burmese does not inflect for number; add “များ” only when the meaning requires it, never after a number: “%lld ရက်”). Keep the tone light and kind, never cheesy or overly poetic.
